<div class="fb-box">
<span class="fb-box-title">This page in one panel</span>
<dl>
<dt>The problem</dt>
<dd>Millions of rows over a design with a modest number of distinct
cells. The model is small; the data are not.</dd>
<dt>In ASReml</dt>
<dd>No direct equivalent. The usual answer is to pre-aggregate by hand
and accept the approximation.</dd>
<dt>In flexyBayes</dt>
<dd><code>flexybayes(..., aggregate = TRUE)</code>, or
<code>flexybayes_stream()</code> for data that never fit in memory.</dd>
<dt>What the posterior adds</dt>
<dd>Nothing different here. The point is that the aggregated fit is
<em>exact</em>, not an approximation, for the models it accepts.</dd>
<dt>What it costs</dt>
<dd>Gaussian identity-link models over factor designs only, and no
per-row quantities afterwards.</dd>
</dl>
</div>

# 1. When the design is small and the data are large

A model over factor predictors partitions the rows into cells. Once the
response is Gaussian with an identity link, everything the likelihood
needs from a cell is three numbers: how many rows, their sum, and their
sum of squares. Those are sufficient statistics.

Two million rows over four hundred cells carry exactly the same
information for that model as four hundred rows of sufficient
statistics. Compressing them is not an approximation and does not
change the posterior -- it changes what has to be held in memory.

This is why the restriction is narrow. Sufficiency of that kind holds
for the Gaussian identity-link case, and the package refuses rather
than compressing where it does not.

# 2. Aggregating in memory


``` r
library(flexyBayes)
set.seed(3)
m  <- 4000
da <- data.frame(f1 = factor(sample(letters[1:6], m, TRUE)),
                 f2 = factor(sample(LETTERS[1:5], m, TRUE)))
da$y <- rnorm(m, 2 + as.integer(da$f1) * 0.3)

fit_a <- flexybayes(y ~ f1 + f2, data = da, backend = "inla",
                    aggregate = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
class(fit_a)[1]
#> [1] "flexybayes_aggregated"
```

The fit reports how far the compression went:


``` r
fit_a$extras$model_info$n_obs
#> [1] 4000
nrow(da)
#> [1] 4000
```

Against the same model fitted on every row:


``` r
fit_full <- flexybayes(y ~ f1 + f2, data = da, backend = "inla",
                       verbose = FALSE)
round(cbind(aggregated = tidy(fit_a)$estimate,
            full_rows  = tidy(fit_full)$estimate), 6)
#>       aggregated full_rows
#>  [1,]   2.287881  2.287881
#>  [2,]   0.279553  0.279553
#>  [3,]   0.644471  0.644471
#>  [4,]   0.975879  0.975879
#>  [5,]   1.222659  1.222659
#>  [6,]   1.553251  1.553251
#>  [7,]  -0.077070 -0.077070
#>  [8,]   0.030843  0.030843
#>  [9,]   0.017906  0.017906
#> [10,]   0.005919  0.005919
```

The coefficients agree to the printed precision, because the aggregated
likelihood is the same likelihood.

# 3. When it refuses

`aggregate = TRUE` is a request, and it is declined rather than silently
downgraded when the compression would not be exact or would not be
worth doing.


``` r
refused <- tryCatch(
  flexybayes(y ~ f1 + f2, data = da[1:40, ], backend = "inla",
             aggregate = TRUE, verbose = FALSE),
  error = function(e) e
)
cat(strwrap(conditionMessage(refused), 72)[1:3], sep = "\n")
#> `aggregate = TRUE` refused by .fb_aggregation_plan():
#> compression_unproductive. Pass aggregate = FALSE for the per-row path.
#> NA
```

The common refusals are a non-Gaussian family, a non-identity link, a
continuous predictor (which gives one cell per row, so nothing
compresses), missing responses (sufficient statistics are not defined
for them), and a design where compression buys too little to be worth
the change of code path.

# 4. Data that never fit in memory

`flexybayes_stream()` takes a file rather than a data frame, reads it in
chunks, accumulates the same per-cell sufficient statistics, and fits
from the accumulator. Peak memory is set by the number of cells, not by
the number of rows.


``` r
flexybayes_stream(
  y ~ f1 + f2,
  file       = "trial_data.csv",
  chunk_size = 1e6,
  backend    = "inla"
)
```

The arithmetic is the same as Section 2. The difference is that the rows
are never all present at once, so a file larger than RAM is fitted
without a database or a sampling step.

# 5. What you give up

An aggregated fit has no rows, so anything defined per row is gone.
There are no residuals against individual observations, no per-row
fitted values, and `augment()` has nothing to append to. Population-level
prediction at the level of the design cells still works.

The fixed-effect and variance-component inference is exactly what the
per-row fit gives. Diagnostics that need per-row quantities are what the
compression costs.

# 6. Pitfalls

**Continuous predictors defeat it.** One distinct value per row means
one cell per row. Bin the covariate first, or fit per-row.

**Missing responses are refused.** Sufficient statistics are not defined
for a missing value, so the aggregated path declines rather than
dropping rows silently.

**Check the compression ratio.** If cells are nearly as numerous as
rows, aggregation adds a code path for no gain, and the package says so
rather than proceeding.

**It is not a sampling method.** No rows are discarded and no subsample
is taken. The whole dataset informs the fit.
